title: InvestED, in order: a Rule #1 course
source: InvestED: The Rule #1 Podcast (Phil Town and Danielle Town), https://feeds.megaphone.fm/investedpodcast

modules.title: Orientation
modules.goal: Why Rule #1 investing, who's teaching, and how the course works.
modules.lesson:
1. **Retirement is a numbers problem you can't outsource to hope.** A typical plan is mostly the house plus a fund returning ~6%; after inflation it can run dry in about five years of drawing income, whereas the same savings at 15% changes the outcome ([029](episodes/029.md)).
2. **Compounding works both ways.** Inflation shrinks spending power and salaries lag it; debt compounds against you too ([030](episodes/030.md)).
3. **The best hedge is owning businesses with pricing power:** a moat lets a company raise prices with inflation.
4. **Manage your own money for three reasons:** moral, financial (you should do better) and practical (it isn't rocket science). Investing is a daily practice, like yoga, that you never finish ([065](episodes/065.md)).
5. **Patience is only possible with your own capital.** Fund managers are judged quarterly and can't sit in cash; you can.
6. Rule #1 (don't lose money) still frames everything; the retirement maths is *why* it matters.

modules.title: Understand the business
modules.goal: Circle of competence, the three circles, reading 10-Ks, and investing in line with your values.
modules.lesson:
Munger's four filters run in order, and **understanding** comes first: if you can't understand the business, stop.

1. **Know your why** ([188](episodes/188.md)): own compounding machines (high returns, reinvested) that outrun inflation, and let your money back only companies you would defend.
2. **Find ideas without throwing darts.** Events, great investors' buys and products you use give names, never decisions ([001](episodes/001.md), [011](episodes/011.md), [016](episodes/016.md), [077](episodes/077.md)). Tips are perishable, but don't rush the homework ([190](episodes/190.md)).
3. **Start inside your circles** ([076](episodes/076.md)): overlap what you love, what you're world-class at and where you make and spend money.
4. **Ignorance is the risk.** Circles grow by connection (Harley to Polaris), but your *feeling* of competence outruns your knowledge, and the edge is where money is lost ([078](episodes/078.md), [079](episodes/079.md), [190](episodes/190.md)).
5. **End every project one of three ways** ([190](episodes/190.md)): no, yes at $X (watch list) or the too-hard box. Wait for a fat pitch.
6. **Run the root-canal test:** if reading about the business is fun, you can learn it. Use the product, read its history, then the 10-K ([017](episodes/017.md)).
7. **Research a company you love in order** ([153](episodes/153.md), Stitch Fix): use it, name the competitors, test the moat, check the track record, then rough out a price. No history means too hard.
8. **Concentrate and dig your canyon;** scuttlebutt plus filings beat many names studied lightly ([085](episodes/085.md)).
9. **Run fashionable assets through the same list** (Bitcoin, [135](episodes/135.md)): no understanding, moat or cash flow means speculation.
10. **Respect the edge** ([150](episodes/150.md)): the costliest error is a business you half-understand. Keep the error checklist short, and invert it.
11. **Next question:** what is the moat, and do the numbers show it?

modules.title: Moats
modules.goal: The five moats (brand, secret, toll bridge, switching, price), how to spot a durable competitive advantage, and how to tell when it's eroding.
modules.lesson:
1. **A moat is an *intrinsic*, *durable* advantage** (Buffett's water around the castle): remove it and the business suffers; rivals with the whole market cap still couldn't win ([003](episodes/003.md)). It is necessary, not sufficient.
2. **Six kinds** ([080](episodes/080.md), [088](episodes/088.md)): brand, toll bridge, price (*lowest cost*, not low price), switching, secrets (patents) and network effect. Earlier notes list five; network effect is a subset of switching. Companies can stack several.
3. **Moats are breachable.** Few companies from 1900 survive, and technology is hard because of creative destruction. Copying erodes them: Whole Foods lost its brand and secret edge once Kroger added organic ranges ([116](episodes/116.md)); USG's brand earns a premium yet overcapacity wrecked returns ([113](episodes/113.md)).
4. **Pricing power is the payoff** ([178](episodes/178.md)): a moat lets a company raise prices when costs rise, so a portfolio of moats resists inflation better than the index. Gold, currency and Bitcoin produce no earnings and can only be speculated on.
5. **Scuttlebutt first:** talk to staff and customers, read the bears and ask competitors why they differ ([080](episodes/080.md)).
6. **Two tests** ([081](episodes/081.md), [082](episodes/082.md)): the numbers (ROE about 10% or better, free cash flow ÷ revenue) and an *obvious* moat. If you must strain to see it, it is too hard. Numbers look out of the back window, and obvious moats are already expensive ([110](episodes/110.md)).
7. **State it in a sentence.** If the 10-K and CEO can't point to the moat, don't invent one ([102](episodes/102.md)). Patagonia's rests on real use by experts, Under Armour's team deals are only marketing ([105](episodes/105.md)).
8. **Replication test:** could you spend the purchase price and build a rival? A moat should survive an idiot, and shouldn't walk out the door with a star ([088](episodes/088.md)).

modules.title: Management
modules.goal: Owner-oriented, honest and capable leaders, and how to judge them from letters, calls and capital allocation.
modules.lesson:
1. **Integrity means integrated:** what you see is what you get. Talent is mainly **capital allocation**: reinvest, acquire, pay out or buy back ([005](episodes/005.md), [100](episodes/100.md)). Think like a sole owner.
2. **Management is where you can still lose everything.** A moat protects against an idiot, not a clever bad actor who loads the company with debt ([089](episodes/089.md), [117](episodes/117.md), [127](episodes/127.md)). Character shows under pressure ([107](episodes/107.md)).
3. **Debt is the real danger** (Horsehead, [075](episodes/075.md)). Years to repay from free cash flow: three at most, and falling ([089](episodes/089.md), [090](episodes/090.md)); [123](episodes/123.md) prefers one to two.
4. **Follow the incentives** ([126](episodes/126.md)): short-tenure bonuses, dilution, reverse splits and voting preferred shares show where owners rank.
5. **Six warning signs** ([089](episodes/089.md)): pay tied to asset size, little own money in the stock, value-destroying acquisitions, shares sold below stated value, a puff-piece letter and EBITDA treated as cash ([102](episodes/102.md)).
6. **Buybacks and acquisitions pass one test:** buy only below value ([100](episodes/100.md)).
7. **Read the words** ([162](episodes/162.md), Rittenhouse): great CEOs write candid letters with facts, detail and admitted mistakes. Clichés and "fog" are a warning; a change in tone can signal a shift in culture or leadership.
8. **Know who the board answers to** ([148](episodes/148.md)): staggered boards and CEO-chosen slates leave shareholders little say, so read the proxy statement and treat entrenchment as a risk.
9. **If you can't meet them, use clues** ([126](episodes/126.md), [127](episodes/127.md)): a founder with a big stake, no debt, and great investors buying. If two people decide everything (Sears), it is too hard. Dual-class shares protect a good founder and shield a poor one ([107](episodes/107.md)).
10. **Refinement:** management matters *less* than the business ([053](episodes/053.md)); [123](episodes/123.md) weights it slightly less for mature moats (jockey versus horse), yet it holds a veto.

modules.title: The numbers: Big Five and ROIC
modules.goal: ROIC, sales, EPS, equity (BVPS) and operating cash flow growth, plus debt, and what they reveal about a moat.
modules.lesson:
1. **ROE (profit ÷ equity) of 10%+ for ten years, not falling, with no debt** is the first proof of a moat ([004](episodes/004.md)). Ten years is long enough for competitors to attack.
2. **Later refinement: ROIC** (return on all invested capital, debt included) is the better number; with no debt, ROE and ROIC match, so Phil simplifies to *avoid debt* ([021](episodes/021.md), [022](episodes/022.md)).
3. **The big four growth rates:** equity (book value) per share, EPS, sales and operating cash flow per share. Look for each at about 10%+ a year and *moving together* ([019](episodes/019.md), [020](episodes/020.md)). Tangled lines (General Motors) mean too hard.
4. **Operating cash flow is the canary** that catches accounting fictions first; EPS is partly a "fiction" of accruals.
5. **Know where each number comes from** ([068](episodes/068.md)): free cash flow isn't a GAAP figure, so two sites can differ. Go to the 10-K and read the notes on odd lines.
6. **The numbers are rear-view.** They show a moat existed; you still must understand why it will last ([023](episodes/023.md)).
7. **Score a real case** ([043](episodes/043.md)): Chipotle against seven numbers. Tech is mostly avoided because moats there erode fast ([022](episodes/022.md)).
8. **Words are data too** ([171](episodes/171.md), [176](episodes/176.md), filed here by the notes; see the management module for [162](episodes/162.md)): Rittenhouse scores CEO letters for candor versus *fog*, counting checkable facts against generalities. A low-fog letter shows an owner of the message, whoever typed it; compare successive CEOs (Home Depot's Blank and Nardelli). Her hub is *capital stewardship*: management that feels *entrusted*, not entitled.

modules.title: Valuation and margin of safety
modules.goal: Sticker Price, the MOS price, Payback Time, Ten Cap and the reasoning behind each.
modules.lesson:
1. **Price is what you pay, value is what you get** ([006](episodes/006.md)). Value is cash that reaches the owner, not accrual "fiction" ([177](episodes/177.md)); compare cash with earnings over ten years ([069](episodes/069.md), [095](episodes/095.md)).
2. **Owner earnings** ([177](episodes/177.md), [181](episodes/181.md), [182](episodes/182.md), [183](episodes/183.md)): net income + depreciation and amortization + change in receivables + change in payables + income tax, less *maintenance* capex. Picture a rented house: rent, minus running costs, minus a roof fund. Operating cash flow ignores maintenance; free cash flow subtracts growth spending too. It is "vaguely right" on purpose, and if you can't finish it you don't understand the business.
3. **Maintenance capex is the art** ([184](episodes/184.md), [186](episodes/186.md)): filings lump it with growth, so read the words ("primarily related to" expansion), use depreciation as a proxy, take the conservative number and stop once more precision can't change the answer. Check third-party capex against the 10-K.
4. **Ten cap** ([146](episodes/146.md), [183](episodes/183.md), [184](episodes/184.md)): owner earnings × 10, a pre-tax 10% yield like a cap rate. It assumes a moat and honest managers. Triangulate with sticker price and payback time: two of three should say on sale.
5. **Sticker price, four inputs** ([009](episodes/009.md), [024](episodes/024.md), [054](episodes/054.md), [121](episodes/121.md)): trailing EPS, ten-year growth, future P/E (lower of twice growth or historical high), 15% MARR. The **windage** growth rate is judgement across 5, 7 and 10 years of the big four. Use the lower of historical and analyst growth ([093](episodes/093.md), [122](episodes/122.md)); analysts' 25% for Fiat Chrysler was absurd ([186](episodes/186.md)).
6. **Buy at half the sticker price** ([010](episodes/010.md), [058](episodes/058.md)), or at most eight years' payback ([008](episodes/008.md), [059](episodes/059.md)). Discounts need a trigger ([121](episodes/121.md)).
7. **Read the gap.** Negative owner earnings, funded by borrowing, flagged Sears years early ([185](episodes/185.md)). A value far above price needs an explanation ([186](episodes/186.md)); too hard is a fine answer.
8. **Reverse-engineer a price:** find the growth it implies ([122](episodes/122.md)). Checklist ([071](episodes/071.md)).
9. **Dividends are not an input** ([066](episodes/066.md)). **Values veto, they don't discount** ([044](episodes/044.md)).

modules.title: Events and buying
modules.goal: Waiting for a business to go on sale, events, buying in tranches and building a watchlist.
modules.lesson:
1. **Mr. Market is moody; you may ignore him** and buy when fear puts a good business on sale ([007](episodes/007.md)). Volatility is not risk.
2. **A good event is temporary and fixable,** at a business you understand and priced clearly below value ([025](episodes/025.md)). A fall that isn't an event is no sale.
3. **System-wide events** (an election, a crash) move price without changing value ([083](episodes/083.md)). Don't trade the vote; use the fear to see whether watch-list names reach a margin-of-safety price.
4. **RULERS** ([012](episodes/012.md)): Radar, Understand, Love, Event, Reduce basis, Story.
5. **Radar has five sources** ([077](episodes/077.md)): scanning tools, gurus' 13F filings, brokers, friends and newsletters. Each gives only a name, to be run through the four filters. Beware inside information.
6. **Buy in tranches** as the price falls, and keep cash as an advantage. Be *anti-fragile*: the investor needs events.
7. **Whole-market gauges** only tell you how hard to hunt, not when ([039](episodes/039.md), [083](episodes/083.md)). [147](episodes/147.md) (early 2018) read them as pricey (market cap about 155% of GDP, Shiller P/E about 32), so wait in cash, "sell mode", with a washtub, and expect a blow-off before the end. It is opinion, not a forecast.
8. **Price what you'd own:** the 10 cap (pay ten times owner earnings, a 10% earnings yield). Owner cash, not reported or "adjusted" earnings, is what you can spend ([147](episodes/147.md)).
9. **Invert the story:** write the bear case first. A drop after buying tests whether you understood.

modules.title: Psychology and practice
modules.goal: Fear, greed, patience, the tension signal, inversion and avoiding noise.
modules.lesson:
1. **Know what you don't know.** Use a margin of safety for errors you can't foresee ([047](episodes/047.md)). Simple is not easy ([087](episodes/087.md)).
2. **Fear drives mass diversification** ([057](episodes/057.md)). The middle path is about 10 companies (20 in a lifetime), 5-10% each, never over ~20%.
3. **Volatility is not risk** ([048](episodes/048.md), [035](episodes/035.md), [104](episodes/104.md), [114](episodes/114.md)). An owner of the cash flow need not sell. A crash is certain, so size for a 50% fall.
4. **Behavioural traps** ([108](episodes/108.md), [115](episodes/115.md)): sunk cost, endowment effect, loss aversion, anchoring, confirmation bias. Antidotes: a checklist and a "Munger" to argue the other side.
5. **How afraid should you be?** Market cap to GDP ~140% and Shiller P/E ~29 say expensive ([106](episodes/106.md)), though Buffett says rates matter most ([113](episodes/113.md)).
6. **Index funds** ([165](episodes/165.md)): an ETF tracks an index, and fees (basis points) eat the return.
7. **Technical indicators are off-canon** ([163](episodes/163.md), [165](episodes/165.md), [166](episodes/166.md)): moving averages, death crosses, MACD and stochastics are "cloud watching". Know them because traders move markets with them; don't use them to buy businesses. Backtests flatter with hindsight.
8. **Practise before money:** paper trade, size by conviction ([014](episodes/014.md), rerun [139](episodes/139.md)). An individual's edge is that nobody forces action ([062](episodes/062.md)).
9. **Stay attached to the story** ([161](episodes/161.md)): ignore the price, not the news. Read the annual report at least, and earnings calls when you can.
10. **Investing is mostly a head game** ([131](episodes/131.md), [132](episodes/132.md), [149](episodes/149.md)): fear and greed are projections about the future, so name the goal, separate fear from evidence, and practise presence.
11. **Build mindset like a muscle** ([096](episodes/096.md), [097](episodes/097.md), [137](episodes/137.md)): gratitude as a *practice*, a calm mind before decisions, and intuition only as trained judgement. Your story about money drives your habits ([152](episodes/152.md)). Investing is a lifelong practice ([155](episodes/155.md)).

modules.title: Portfolio and selling
modules.goal: Concentration, position sizing, when the story changes, and when to sell.
modules.lesson:
1. **Rank asset buckets by what they produce:** bonds are low risk and low return; gold and currency are hedges or too-hard bets ([036](episodes/036.md)); commodities have no moat ([037](episodes/037.md), [038](episodes/038.md)); annuities bet on your lifespan ([031](episodes/031.md)).
2. **Fees, taxes and misaligned incentives** destroy compounding in mutual funds ([015](episodes/015.md)).
3. **Passive versus active** ([130](episodes/130.md)): index funds cost ~0.1-0.25% against 1-2% and suit people who won't do the work.
4. **Risk, two definitions** ([094](episodes/094.md)): beta versus company risk; market-wide moves are weather.
5. **Reduce basis** ([026](episodes/026.md)): dividends return capital until the holding acts like a growing "equity bond". A dividend is only as safe as owner cash flow and low debt ([028](episodes/028.md), [066](episodes/066.md)).
6. **Wait for the fat pitch** ([124](episodes/124.md)): fund managers must keep swinging; you needn't. Cash is a position ([072](episodes/072.md)); bring a washtub, not a thimble.
7. **Read the weather, don't forecast it** ([156](episodes/156.md), [157](episodes/157.md)): Buffett indicator, Shiller PE, interest rates and Buffett's record cash all say expensive, but Phil calls it opinion. Technical signals are trading tools, not canon.
8. **Sell at intrinsic value** ([158](episodes/158.md), [159](episodes/159.md), [160](episodes/160.md)): intrinsic value is the present value of future cash (roughly right beats precisely wrong). Buffett's 1961 partnership letter sold bargains once they re-priced, because the return came from the mispricing and fades. The cash is the washtub for the next crash. *Refinement:* great compounders may be held instead; holding at value costs capital "velocity".
9. **Shorting and speculation** ([160](episodes/160.md)): Buffett and Munger avoid shorts; Tesla-style stories lack reasonable certainty of cash flow.
10. **Options are a racehorse** ([167](episodes/167.md), [168](episodes/168.md), [169](episodes/169.md)): a collar (own the stock, buy a put, sell a call) bounds a gain, but learn the business first. Inverted yield curves warn of recession; real value investors are rare.

modules.title: The masters
modules.goal: Buffett, Munger, Graham, Pabrai, Spier and others: their ideas and their records.
modules.lesson:
1. **Dhandho** ([013](episodes/013.md)): asymmetric bets, small loss if wrong, large gain if right; Pabrai's "free lottery tickets" ([098](episodes/098.md), [099](episodes/099.md)). Size by conviction; diversification is for those who don't know.
2. **Graham to Munger** ([063](episodes/063.md), [098](episodes/098.md), [141](episodes/141.md), [164](episodes/164.md), [173](episodes/173.md)): Graham's net-nets meant 100-200 bargains; Buffett and Munger wait for a few wonderful businesses on sale. Graham's real shift was seeing a share as part of a business ([174](episodes/174.md)).
3. **Patience and fees shape behaviour** ([101](episodes/101.md), [120](episodes/120.md), [144](episodes/144.md), [172](episodes/172.md)): Pabrai charges no management fee, only a share above a hurdle, while asset-based fees reward gathering assets and shadowing the index. Institutions can't sit out; Buffett closed his partnership in 1969 rather than play a game he didn't understand ([174](episodes/174.md)).
4. **Be a consumer of stocks** ([172](episodes/172.md)): if you keep adding capital, lower prices are good.
5. **Work alone, from facts** ([174](episodes/174.md), [175](episodes/175.md)): distance from Wall Street, share facts not opinions, and expect confirmation bias to hide red flags. Temperament beats IQ.
6. **Build a checklist from other people's errors** ([175](episodes/175.md)): Pabrai's ~150 questions are mostly debt, management and moat. Run every item yourself.
7. **Don't copy a guru's buy** ([173](episodes/173.md)): you miss the exit and the reasoning, and cheap may stay cheap. Foreign firms add macro, currency and auditor risk.
8. **Index funds are for those who won't do the work** ([189](episodes/189.md)). Buffett's 2007 bet was against a fund of funds; size handicaps him, not you.
9. **Using gurus** ([138](episodes/138.md), [141](episodes/141.md), [143](episodes/143.md), [145](episodes/145.md), [164](episodes/164.md)): curate a short list, read 13Fs for quarterly change (up to 45 days late, silent on cash and shorts; [140](episodes/140.md), [144](episodes/144.md)). Look for 50%+ top-five concentration and *practice shares*. Munger's ideas: clone great investors, buy share-count shrinkers, buy spin-offs. Then do your own work.
10. **Model, don't copy** ([086](episodes/086.md)); test: does the return hold if nothing wonderful happens ([042](episodes/042.md))?

modules.title: Case studies and interviews
modules.goal: Companies analysed on the show, and guests' stories and lessons.
modules.lesson:
1. **Real assets obey Rule #1** ([033](episodes/033.md)): understand them, find a durable edge, buy after a bust.
2. **Run the filters on a name** ([103](episodes/103.md), [105](episodes/105.md), [154](episodes/154.md)): Under Armour has an okay moat and negative free cash flow; Blue Apron fails in minutes. **Debt kills** (Horsehead, [075](episodes/075.md)). Debt repayable from two years of free cash flow is fine, three the edge, four too much ([187](episodes/187.md)).
3. **Love is not price** ([179](episodes/179.md)): Amazon was a wonderful business, but about $8B of free cash flow against a $1T value was not defensible. A "starter tranche" of an overpriced stock is just a bet the market rises, and becomes dead money if it falls. A real position is 10-20%; a token one is a practice share ([187](episodes/187.md)).
4. **A news-driven price move is not a change in value** ([180](episodes/180.md)): Nike moved on an ad while the business was unchanged. Fashion is less predictable than food; labels like B Corp are shortcuts, so read what the company does.
5. **Whole Foods, start to finish** ([116](episodes/116.md), [118](episodes/118.md), [119](episodes/119.md), [125](episodes/125.md), [191](episodes/191.md), [192](episodes/192.md), [193](episodes/193.md)): a price moat is fragile against a rival that can lose money. A year proves little (the 10-10 rule); judge the *story*, not the price. Ask "will it grow at all?" rather than how fast; Kroger's ~3% margins signal no moat, and a CEO's sudden exit is a red flag. Disruption is slow.
6. **Disruptors fail the tools** ([128](episodes/128.md)), and **crypto is speculation** ([133](episodes/133.md), [134](episodes/134.md), [136](episodes/136.md)). Young firms need a pre-IPO history, or sit in a small "risky business" slice ([187](episodes/187.md)).
7. **Teach and defend one stock** ([170](episodes/170.md)); risk tolerance mostly reflects education ([151](episodes/151.md)); money is a vote ([056](episodes/056.md)). Wealth is more than money ([142](episodes/142.md), [194](episodes/194.md)).

glossary.definition: Don't lose money. Rule #2: don't forget Rule #1 (Buffett).
Meaning (understand it), Moat, Management, Margin of safety: Munger's four filters, applied in order.
The set of businesses you truly understand. Knowing where it ends matters more than how big it is.
Temporary bad news that puts a good business on sale.
Buying far enough below value (Rule #1: 50% of Sticker) that mistakes don't lose you money.
Making the best case against your idea, then rebutting it or walking away.
Buffett's thought experiment: only 20 purchases in a lifetime, so each must count.
Ideas you pass on because you can't understand them well enough.
A durable competitive advantage: brand, secrets, switching, toll bridge or low cost.
Return on equity: profit divided by shareholders' equity. Rule #1 wants 10%+ for ten years.
Return on invested capital: profit on all capital, debt included. Better than ROE once debt is in play.
Equity (book value), EPS, sales and operating cash flow per share, each ideally growing 10%+ together.
Phil's estimate of value today: grow EPS ten years, apply a future P/E, discount at 15%.
Minimum acceptable rate of return: 15% a year in Rule #1.
Years of cash flow needed to earn back the price paid. About eight or fewer is a fair price.
Net earnings minus maintenance capex: the cash an owner could take out.
First-year cash return on purchase price; the price test for real estate and cash-flow businesses.
Graham's moody business partner who quotes a price daily; you may ignore him.
The theory that price already reflects all information. Rule #1 relies on it failing in the short run.
Modern portfolio theory calls price movement risk; Rule #1 says a falling price on unchanged value lowers risk.
Lower the money at risk in a holding by taking cash back, such as dividends.
A business whose cash payout to you grows over time, like a bond whose coupon keeps rising.
Radar, Understand, Love, Event, Reduce basis, Story: Phil's checklist.
A narrow area you study deeply: an inch wide and a mile deep.
Gathering information from customers, employees, suppliers and competitors.
Gujarati for endeavours that create wealth: low-risk, high-uncertainty bets (Pabrai).
Real estate investment trust: a listed company owning property that passes income to shareholders.
A contract paying income for life; essentially a bet on your lifespan that inflation erodes.
Cash generated by running the business; catches accounting fictions first.
Ability to raise prices without losing customers; the inflation hedge.
Valuing a holding at today's quoted price rather than its value.
Cash from operations minus purchase of property and equipment; the cash left for owners. Not a GAAP number, so sources differ.
Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual return in percent; also the quick way to discount a future value.
Tangible book value (equity minus goodwill and intangibles): what the business is worth dead. Taught in 060, later dropped as a method.
Graham's very cheap, low-quality company that gives one last puff of profit; Munger steered Buffett to wonderful businesses instead.
The latest four quarters combined; the earnings base for the sticker price.
The pressure on professional managers to match the crowd and show results every quarter, so they cannot wait in cash.
Purchase price minus cash already returned (dividends); shows the risk still outstanding.
Buying something dear in the hope that someone else will pay more; the logic of bubbles.
Investing a fixed sum on a schedule regardless of price; Phil calls it a bet that the market rises.
Buffett's borrowed baseball idea: there are no called strikes, so wait for an obvious opportunity inside the zone you understand.
A moat where the only alternative is far costlier, usually a physical or regulatory monopoly (railroad lines, utilities). Hard to hold without regulation.
Being the lowest-cost producer, so you survive price wars and troughs that shut others down. Matters most in commodity businesses.
How much a stock tends to move relative to the market (1.0 = the market). Modern portfolio theory's measure of risk; Phil ignores it.
Taleb's term for something that gains from shocks. Rule #1 investing needs panics to buy wonderful companies on sale.
Years of free cash flow needed to repay the debt. About three at most, and falling.
Ask whether reading about a business and its industry is fun or a root canal; fun suggests you can learn it.
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. Buffett and Munger call it a delusion because it ignores real costs of keeping the business running.
The growth rate you choose by judgement after studying all four growth numbers over 5, 7 and 10 years, not a simple average.
Buffett's image of holding cash for the storm that rains gold: a bucket, not a thimble.
Owning something makes you value it above what you would pay for it, so selling feels like a loss.
Money already spent is gone either way and should not change whether you hold or sell.
Buying a stock trading below a takeover price to collect the gap: speculation with an edge, not Rule #1 investing.
Share classes with unequal votes that give founders or families control; check what voting power you are buying.
Total US stock value divided by GDP; Buffett called 70-80% fine and 100% playing with fire.
Clinging to a price or past view after the facts change; the cure is to recheck your homework.
Quick valuation: free cash flow times 10 (a 10% cash yield) as a rough fair market cap.
Fewer shares, each worth proportionally more; changes nothing by itself but is often used after steep falls and dilution (DryShips).
A stock bought because its assets are worth more than its price; it depends on management realising the value (Sears).
A low-cost fund that copies an index (about 0.1-0.25% a year against 1-2% for active funds); Buffett's advice for those who won't learn to invest.
A ledger shared across many computers so records are hard to change; the technology is investable through companies, a coin is not.
Initial coin offering: a sale of new tokens, often on only a white paper.
Buying for a price rise without a way to value the asset's cash flow (Bitcoin, a Picasso, tulips).
Quarterly report of long US stock holdings by managers with over $100 million; up to 45 days late and silent on cash and shorts.
Borrowing shares, selling them and hoping to buy back cheaper; losses are theoretically unlimited.
A long/short pairing meant to profit whichever way the market moves; hard because it needs two right answers.
A fund holding longs and shorts, so its 13F overstates its exposure.
A tiny position used to force yourself to follow a company while you learn it.
Phil's concentration test: the top five holdings should be at least about half the portfolio.
A tradable right to buy shares at a fixed price before an expiry date; it carries a clock.
Earnings per share divided by price; the inverse of P/E. A 10 cap is a 10% earnings yield.
Cash an owner can take out after maintaining the business: net income + D&A + change in receivables and payables + income tax, less maintenance capex. Preferred to reported or adjusted earnings.
Directors elected in overlapping terms, so only a few seats are up each year; it can entrench weak management.
Annual filing listing what shareholders vote on, including board nominees and executive pay.
Attending to the present moment on purpose; a way to see facts instead of fear and greed.
Automated service that invests your money, usually in broad funds, for a small percentage fee.
Your written case for owning a company: its mission, moat, management and price.
Customers stay because leaving is costly or painful.
How long cash and borrowing can fund a company's losses.
Total market value divided by GDP.
Price divided by the ten-year, inflation-adjusted average of earnings (CAPE).
A calculation from price and volume history used to predict direction; not part of the Buffett-Munger approach.
Present value of the cash a business will generate; the book calls it the sticker price.
Call where management explains results and answers analysts; Phil treats it as best practice alongside the annual report.
Rittenhouse's measure of fact-deficient, obfuscating generalities in management letters.
The 50-day moving average crossing below the 200-day (the golden cross is the reverse).
A price below current assets minus all liabilities; Graham-style bargain.
A company buying and retiring its own shares; Munger favours companies that shrink their share count.
A parent distributing shares of a subsidiary to its holders.
Exchange-traded fund: tracks an index and trades like a stock.
Moving average convergence divergence: a momentum gauge comparing fast and slow moving averages.
Momentum indicator flagging overbought (above 80) and oversold (below 20) readings.
Owning a stock, buying a put and selling a call to bound the outcome.
Right to sell at a set price by a set date.
Right to buy at a set price by a set date.
Cutoff: buy before it to receive the next dividend.
Plain, specific, accountable communication: Rittenhouse's "courage to shine light into dark places".
Managing owners' money as a trustee; "entrusted, not entitled". The hub of Rittenhouse's seven-system model.
Buffett's stance that a buyer who keeps adding capital wants lower prices, as a hamburger buyer does.
The minimum return a fund must beat before its manager takes a share of profits; Pabrai's alternative to an asset-based fee.
Favouring evidence that supports what you already think; the more time you put in, the harder red flags are to see.
Recording sales and expenses when earned or incurred, not when cash moves, so a profitable company can still run out of cash.
Spending needed to keep the business where it is; growth capex raises output. Filings report only the total.
Capital stuck in a stock that must recover its loss before it earns again; cash held for a crash can beat it.
A private certification for socially minded companies that the company pays for; not a legal form.
Restates net income into cash across operating, investing and financing activities; owner earnings draws on the first two.
Money customers owe the company, and money it owes suppliers; a fall in receivables or rise in payables adds cash.
The owner must put in cash to keep the business going, as Sears did for years, funded by borrowing.
Personal exposure to the outcome of your decisions; a small real position sharpens attention.
A small part of the portfolio for companies without a full record, kept small.
A business that reinvests earnings at a high return and compounds faster than inflation.
A fund that invests in other funds, so investors pay two layers of fees; the target of Buffett's 2007 bet.
Sales growth at stores open at least a year; a retail and restaurant measure that transfers between industries.
Don't hold anything for 10 minutes that you wouldn't hold for 10 years.
An investment bought at a price where you expect your money back, so any big win is a bonus (Pabrai).
